body.content: If you have been active in the aim training community at any point over the past
four years or so, something like this should be pretty familiar to you.
These are the voltaic benchmarks and going back as far as I can remember,
these have been considered the default way to test your skill when training.
Over time they have taken on a bit of a different role though,
with the benchmarks themselves becoming the training tool,
not just something to test your skill with.
I imagine a lot of you are probably expecting me to say something about how awful that is
and how grinding the benchmarks is bad for improvement and it certainly can be but
I don't think it has to be.
The voltaic benchmarks have continued to be iterated upon over the years but
there was never any question about what they were being designed to do.
They were to test aiming skill in a way that paints the most complete picture possible,
something that they have become very good at.
Other benchmarks have been made over the years too but in my experience,
most of them are either structurally identical to voltaic's benchmarks or hyper-focused on a
specific category.
And that's not to say that all of these are bad or anything but I wanted to try something
a little different.
These are the viscose benchmarks and the idea they started from was,
what if a benchmark was designed to be a training tool?
My goal was to essentially trick people into playing scenarios that are good for practice
instead of just good for evaluating your own skill level.
What this means is that they might not be as consistent as voltaic's benchmarks or cover
as many areas of aim but instead they focus on the scenarios and categories that I have
found the most useful to my own personal aim development no matter the game I'm playing.
The skill targets are slapped on as a motivator but they aren't really the point.
The goal here instead is to develop strong fundamentals and good technique which will
transfer over to any game.
You can play other game specific training methods on top of using these to benchmark
if you'd like to as well but I have tried to cover everything here.
If you want to give them a try now there's a link to the spreadsheet in the description.
Go on to file, make a copy and you're good to go.
But I want to address how these actually differ from voltaic's benchmarks and how
do those differences better facilitate improving your technique.
I think the biggest factor is the categorization of scenarios.
Here are voltaics focusing primarily on the type of aim involved with even numbers of scenarios
for each type.
The thing is though the main three types of aim are not equally important for in-game translation
and some very important scenario types like pokeball are entirely absent here
since they don't really fit into any of these categories
plus in my opinion target switching is fairly overrepresented.
What I've done instead is distribute the scenarios unevenly based on what I have
personally found the most useful for in-game translation
and split those scenarios into more technique focused categories.
So instead of categorizing tasks based on what they are I group them based on what they do.
There is no target switching subcategory anymore.
Those scenarios all fall under flicking technique and are subdivided into which area
of your flicks they focus on.
Same with control tracking being split into which muscle group the scenario targets.
This both gives you an idea of how to approach each scenario
as well as what area you're weak at if you are struggling with specific ones.
For example a lower relative score on the fingertip subcategory in control tracking
doesn't just tell you general info like work on tracking.
It is very specifically a weakness with fine control over small movements
either with your fingertips or wrists depending on grip and play style.
And while I have designed the benchmarks in a way where grinding the scenarios you
are weak at will help you address those weaknesses.
If you want to vary your practice more you can pick out extra scenarios to help isolate the issue.
How I like to do this is just by searching for the name of the base scenario to find variants.
For example clover raw control.
Typing that in brings up heaps of versions of the scenario with slight variations like
slower, faster, larger, adding blinks and each change will help work on different things.
You can also check out other benchmarks on this website that have more narrow
focuses than mine or look through Vltag's recommended scenario list
or just playlists other people have made to find scenarios that will help you improve
the areas you're weakest in.
About playlists though I've heard that a lot of people play these benchmarks as if
they were one and this isn't something I recommend personally.
You can if you'd like to and I'm sure it is still beneficial but in my opinion the value
in benchmarks is that they make it easy for you to motivate yourself to push yourself to
improve category by category.
How I approach every task is a test of optimization.
What am I doing wrong from a technique perspective that this scenario is forcing me to improve at?
The most recent example for me was passu.
I wasn't leading my shots properly and trying to push my score further forced me to improve my
technique.
For me this is what makes benchmarks better than playlists and why I chose to make this
list of scenarios into one instead of just posting it as a playlist.
By encouraging you to look at your score on each scenario, set a goal for yourself and
figure out what is preventing you technique wise from reaching it is why I think benchmarks have
become such a good tool to improve.
It prevents you from autopiloting and forces you to actively analyze your own improvement
which is exactly what I wanted when making these and dictated every decision from some
category names to rank difficulty.
On that note, the most common question I've been asked about this benchmark is why is x
ranked so hard if it is on the easier benchmarks?
A lot of people have told me that fuchsia is way way harder than wool
even though fuchsia is classified as medium and wool is hard and they are right.
This is an intentional design change from Voltaic and actually something I suggested
to them during the development of season 5.
I think the best way to think of it is that these terms, easier, medium and hard,
represent the difficulty of the scenarios included in the benchmarks.
Not this go required for any given rank on those benchmarks.
There will be players here I would consider advanced who can't get to the top rank on the
medium scenarios here and that isn't just to make these benchmarks really hard for no reason.
The Voltaic benchmarks have had a bit of a problem where the jumps between difficulties
is so drastic that it feels completely impossible to broach for a lot of people.
When trying to go from master to grandmaster you need to not only get a better score but
get that score on a significantly harder scenario.
I think this is why master became cited as the cutoff point for when aim trainers lose their
value even though this isn't true in my opinion.
It's just that the time investment required per rank grows so much after this point
partially because you have to get those scores on increasingly difficult scenarios.
What I've done to try and alleviate this issue is to have roughly two ranks of overlap
for each difficulty.
So ordering the ranks in terms of how hard they're supposed to be would look something like this.
This means that while someone is climbing to the higher ranks on the medium scenarios,
for example, they can try out the harder ones and still have scores to shoot for there.
In my opinion, less challenging scenarios always have their place when aim training no
matter how good you get.
I think of easiest scenarios as refinement of your technique and harder scenarios as
a stress test of that technique.
You really should be playing both simultaneously and this isn't something that conventional
benchmarks encourage.
Once you're done with intermediate on voltaic, you move on to advanced, whereas here it's
highly encouraged to keep playing the set of benchmarks below the highest set you can get
scores on.
I'm not too far off so complete on these and I still get a lot of value from playing
the medium difficulty scenarios.
This is also a part of the reason why there are so many ranks here but not the only reason.
Another goal I had with these was to make starting out on them more approachable than voltaic.
I want most people who are brand new to aim training to be able to get a rank in a couple
of tries.
This means that there are a lot more ranks on the easiest scenarios than voltaic has and
since medium overlaps with the easier and harder scenarios there is a bunch of ranks there too.
As for the ranks themselves, I have strayed away from voltaic's contemporary energy system
and went back to their old system of requiring one score per subcategory to get a rank.
My reasoning for this is twofold.
Making people play a wider range of scenarios will naturally lead to them becoming more
well rounded and it also allows the individual score targets to be lower for each.
Since you can get a rank in voltaic with only three to four scores in that rank total,
the individual scores are going to be a grind.
Whereas here, you need at least 14 scores, meaning even if I want fuchsia to be equal
to voltaic nova as a rank, the fuchsia score targets can be much more reachable which I
personally find more motivating.
I think that's everything I have to say about the benchmarks themselves but if you'd like
to know more about how to play each scenario specifically, I'm working on adding these little
notes to each scenario when you click it with the link to a void as well as a small write up.
And if you want more information, I should have a video up on my second channel by the time this
goes live talking through similar things with my own and Matty's gameplay to demonstrate
what proper technique looks like for each.
Also, thank you so much to Pingua5 for making the spreadsheet for this.
A lot of my stupid ideas like bringing back vaults or having a seemingly random number
of scenarios per some category would not have worked at all using a benchmark template.
And I love the rank names and color scheme which are all Pingu's doing.
Please show them your support in the comments and thanks for watching.
